There's two types of games - Boffer and Salon.

Boffer games use foam-padded weapons, and have live, real-time combat. They tend to be more "action" oriented.

Salon games use abstracted rules to resolve conflict, like drawing cards or a quick round of rock-paper-scissors. They tend to be more "social" oriented.

This isn't to say that all boffer games are non-stop action and can't include politics/scheming/backstabbing, nor is it to say that salon games are nothing but boring politics without exciting fight scenes. They just tend towards certain narratives and actions due to how they're constructed.

That said, there are some basics that all games share:

  1. All games have a system of rules that are used to interact with the game world. Just like a tabletop Dungeons & Dragons game, how you do stuff is governed by rules.

  2. You make and then play a character. It's usually the same character the whole event, and that same character usually persists between games, too.
